Research master's degrees are primarily research based, although may contain taught elements, particularly on research methods.
Specialised or advanced study master's degrees are primarily taught degrees, although commonly at least a third of the course is devoted to a research project assessed by dissertation.

Professional or practice master's degrees are designed to prepare students for a particular professional career and are primarily taught, although they may include work placements and independent study projects.
Research master's degrees in the US require the completion of taught courses, examinations, and a research thesis, typically taking two years.
Professional master's degrees may be structured like research master's or may concentrate on a specific discipline, often substituting a project for the thesis.
In the UK, postgraduate master's degrees typically take one to two years full-time or two to four years part-time.
In Australia, master's degrees vary from one year for a 'research' or 'coursework' master's to four years for an 'extended' master's degree.
A 'second cycle' master's degree programme is typically 90–120 ECTS credits, with at least 60 ECTS credits at second-cycle level.
Admission to a master's degree normally requires successful completion of study at bachelor's degree level.
Students will normally have to write a personal statement.
In arts and humanities, students will often have to submit a portfolio of work.
In the UK, students will normally need to have a 2:1.
Graduate schools in the US may require students to take standardized tests, such as the GRE, GMAT, or LSAT.
